title: Pressure-cooker beef bourguignon
subtitle: A French classic condensed into a weekday meal
excerpt: Beef chuck braised in red wine with lardons, mushrooms, and pearl onions, pressure-cooked until the beef yields completely. A 3-hour dish brought within reach of a weeknight.
sourceNotes: Boeuf bourguignon is documented in Julia Child's Mastering the Art of French Cooking (1961) and is derived from the Burgundy peasant tradition of braising tough beef cuts in local wine. The original method takes 3 to 4 hours in the oven.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in airtight containers for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge. Reheat gently; add a splash of stock if the sauce has thickened too much.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dish tastes better the next day. Refrigerate overnight, lift off the fat, and reheat gently on the hob.

content.text: Beef bourguignon is a French braise: beef chuck cooked in red wine until the collagen breaks down and the meat yields in chunky, softened pieces. The pressure cooker compresses the long oven time into a 35 to 40-minute cook at high pressure, producing tender beef with a sauce that has the depth of something cooked for hours.

Brown everything properly before sealing the lid. Lardons, beef, and mushrooms all need separate turns in a hot pan, this is the step that gives the dish its colour and flavour and cannot be skipped. The pressure cooker cannot add browning; it can only cook what you put in.
Use a decent red wine, something you would drink. Burgundy or a robust Côtes du Rhône works well. The wine does not need to be expensive, but it should taste good.

Heat a large frying pan over medium-high heat. Add the lardons and cook for 4 minutes until they render their fat and colour. Remove with a slotted spoon. In the same pan, cook the halved mushrooms without stirring for 3 minutes until browned. Remove and set aside with the lardons.

Season the beef chunks with salt and pepper. Add {{olive-oil}} of olive oil to the pan, raise the heat to high, and sear the beef in two batches for 3 minutes per side until deeply browned. Transfer to the pressure cooker.

Reduce the heat to medium. Add the shallots and garlic; cook for 2 minutes. Add {{tomato-puree}} of tomato puree and stir. Pour in {{red-wine}} of red wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping the base of the pan. Add {{stock-beef}} of beef stock. Pour everything into the pressure cooker. Add the lardons, mushrooms, thyme, and bay.

Seal the lid and bring to high pressure. Cook at high pressure for 35 minutes. Allow a natural pressure release of 10 minutes, then quick-release any remaining pressure. Open the lid and check the beef, it should break apart when pressed. If not, cook for a further 10 minutes.
If the sauce is thin, set the open pressure cooker on the hob over medium heat and simmer for 8 to 10 minutes until it thickens slightly. Discard the thyme and bay. Taste and adjust the seasoning.

rows.symptom: The beef is tough after cooking
rows.cause: Insufficient cooking time, or the cooker did not reach full pressure.
rows.fix: Return to high pressure for a further 15 minutes. Beef chuck is very forgiving, longer cooking only improves it.

rows.cause: Red wine produces more liquid than the recipe accounts for when the vegetables have high water content.
rows.fix: Simmer the sauce in the open pot for 10 to 15 minutes at a brisk boil until it coats the back of a spoon. You can also mix 1 tablespoon of cornflour with 2 tablespoons of cold water and stir through the simmering sauce.

rows.symptom: The wine flavour is too raw
rows.cause: The wine was not simmered for long enough in the pan before going into the pressure cooker.
rows.fix: Next time, let the wine bubble for a full 3 minutes before adding the stock. You can also add a pinch of sugar to balance remaining acidity.

rows.symptom: The shallots have dissolved into the sauce
rows.cause: Small shallots break down under pressure during a long cook.
rows.fix: This is not a problem, the shallots thicken the sauce. For a version with whole shallots visible in the dish, add them only in the last 15 minutes of cooking.

content.text: Bourguignon improves overnight. Refrigerate uncovered until cold, then cover and store for up to 3 days. The fat can be lifted off when cold. Freeze in airtight portions for up to 3 months. Serve with boiled potatoes, noodles, or crusty bread.

Beef bourguignon moved from French peasant cooking into English-speaking kitchens largely through Julia Child in the 1960s. It became shorthand for achievable French home cooking. The pressure-cooker version makes no claim on authenticity. It simply puts the dish within reach on a weeknight.
